newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian cocoa stocks leave some shippers short.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian cocoa stocks leave some shippers short.

text.p: Ivorian port cocoa stocks stand at about 150,000 tonnes after busy March exports but some shippers remain short of cocoa for May contracts as arrivals dwindle, exporters and industry sources said on Thursday.
Port arrivals of 1996/97 cocoa (Oct-Sept) totalled 970-980,000 by April 14 (since Oct 1) as the main crop (Oct-April) grinds to a close, with an estimated 770,000 tonnes exported by mid-April.
"Total exports are about that (770,000) but SICC (Ivorian exporter) is about to ship another 10,000 tonnes," said one port source.
"Local processors will need up to 160,000 tones this year so they will have taken about 80,000 tonnes by now," said another.

Official shipping data showed total bean exports to end-February totalled just under 600,000 tonnes. Bean shipment data for San Pedro show March exports of 52,000 tonnes but volumes leaving Abidjan have not been compiled.
Product exports up to March amounted to 30,000 tonnes but beans lose 20 percent of their weight during processing and stocks of cocoa remain at factory warehouses.
One Ivorian forwarder, which exports roughly one third of annual cocoa arrivals, handled 50,000 tonnes in March.

Some of Ivory Coast's largest cocoa exporters, including Jean-Abile Gal and SICC have recently been looking to make up cocoa export volumes. Others, including Ivory Coast's largest exporter, SIFCA, and trader ED & F Man's export arm Tropival held larger stocks, sources told Reuters.
Exporters said recent world cocoa price rises had helped spur an April scramble for cocoa while others had bought May contracts from the Caistab without enough physicals for shipment.
Port arrivals dwindled to up to 5,000 tonnes/week in early April, against 8,000 in the record 1.2 million tonnes 1995/96 year. Mid-April arrivals last year reached 1.03 million tonnes.
Port sources said most arrivals were still exportable, although bean sizes were slipping in some areas to below the 105 beans/100 grammes export standard as the midcrop (May-Sept) season approaches.
Sources said one exporter supplying Cargill and U.S.-based trader Phibro had been short of 20,000 tonnes of cocoa.
"Next year will be an open trading year but Ivory Coast will still have to ship this year to meet its contracts with Phibro," said the source.
Ivory Coast's Caistab currently sets aside a proportion of its auction sales for direct contracts with foreign traders. Auction trade records are not published.
Discussions on market reforms have included plans to alter or end the arrangement in 1997/98 to give preference to Ivory Coast-based exporters.
